paras: The attempted lynching of Lawson Simril took place in Ebernezer Township, apparently in South Carolina, on Wednesday, 6 August 1890, when a crowd of neighbors seized and bound Simril, a Black man accused of entering a young woman's room at night, and resolved to execute him. A local man persuaded the crowd to let the law take its course, and Simril was jailed the next morning to await trial. The Lexington Dispatch reported it as a "Narrow Escape From Lynching."

According to the Dispatch, on the preceding Sunday night someone raised a window, entered a young woman's room while she slept, and caught hold of her hand. She woke, saw "a colored man" beside her, and raised the alarm, and he jumped from the window and escaped in the dark. The house had recently been painted, and the family kept quiet, hoping the paint would furnish a clue.

A few days later Lawson Simril, who had been employed and partly raised on the place, appeared in the yard with fresh paint on his trousers. Neighbors were told, the alarm "spread like wildfire," and a crowd soon gathered and apprehended him with little trouble. The crowd bound Simril and, in the paper's words, "had decided upon executing him at once."
An "influential gentleman of the neighborhood" then arrived and begged the crowd to let the law take its course, and they finally agreed.

Simril was taken to jail the following morning to await trial. The Dispatch stated that he admitted to the gentleman that he had entered the room but said he had been looking for money. No report of a trial or of action against the crowd appears in the coverage.

The only report found is a local item in the Lexington Dispatch of 13 August 1890. The paper wrote that "but for some cool heads that community would have scored a lynching," crediting restraint while treating the accusation, which it called a "felonious attempt" on the young woman, and the paint evidence as settled.
No other white paper and no Black newspaper was found reporting the episode.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Lawson Simril
bases: A crowd seized and bound Lawson Simril, a Black man accused of entering a young woman's room, and decided to execute him before being persuaded to hand him to the law (A1): an attempted lynching.

Simril was not killed; a crowd acting without authority bound him and decided to execute him over an alleged attack on a young woman, but agreed to let the law take its course and he was jailed (A1). It is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.
Only the Lexington Dispatch's local item reports the episode (A1); no other account was found in either press.

accounts.label: Local newspaper report
accounts.gist: A man entered a sleeping young woman's room and fled; paint on Lawson Simril's trousers days later led neighbors to seize and bind him and resolve to execute him, until a local gentleman persuaded them to give him to the law.

accounts.label: Simril's statement (as reported)
accounts.gist: Simril is reported to have acknowledged entering the room but to have claimed he was looking for money.

framing.detail: The Lexington Dispatch headlined a 'Narrow Escape From Lynching' and praised the 'cool heads' who stopped it, while presenting the accusation (a 'felonious attempt') and the paint evidence as established.
